newsitem.title: UK: EU tender takes steam out of domestic grains market.
newsitem.headline: EU tender takes steam out of domestic grains market.

text.p: Thursday's lacklustre EU export tender took the impetus out of Europe's domestic cereals market, despite noises from officials that it was not the first sign of a new trend.

The EU's cereals management committee granted wheat export licences of 91,200 tonnes compared with 300,000-400,000 tonnes in recent weeks. But EU sources point out that the first meeting after the holiday and a break last week, took place in the absence of some key figures.
It should not be used as a pointer by those trying to get an idea of future EU export policy, they said.

Some blamed the presence of U.S. Agriculture Department General Sales Manager Chris Goldthwait in Brussels for a meeting with officials for the timid award, although member state officials doubted whether there was any real effect. However, "it wasn't a day for messing around with a USDA delegation in town," one said.
Combined with a fall in US prices on Friday, the tender leaves EU wheat in a very poor competitive position on the world market, trade analysts said.
Although export concerns have weighed on prices, fears that the new crop is not getting enough water proved a bullish element in France, the UK and Spain.

"The market's getting worried about the weather. The crops need water," one French broker said. It meant that although the EU tender put a stop to rises in French new crop prices, sellers were not ready to mark prices down at least until it rains.
French old crop buyers held back after the EU tender, but sellers decided to back away from the market, rather than cut prices, traders said. The result was a quiet end to the week.
German wheat markets held firm after the EU tender, traders said. Sellers were holding on to supply and domestic buying was muted.
"There are no French and British imports because their prices are above ours and there is little domestic demand, but we're looking for buyers in western and southern Europe," one broker said.
Feed rye and barley were offered into intervention but bread rye prices benefitted from some sales to south eastern Europe.

One British trader called the market a "roller coaster" this week. It started firm, pumped up a week ago by export optimism and buoyed by concerns over the possible effect of dry weather on the UK and Spanish crops.
It got to highs and market players started to get the idea it might be a little overdone. "If we're more expensive than France where are we going to export to?" the trader said.
"Then it came flying back down again," he said. LIFFE May wheat's high on April 1 was 102.85 stg. On Friday it saw a low of 97.25 stg.

This volatility has helped divorce the futures, and the fob and delivered markets from one another, the trader said. Cash grains traders complained that it made pricing difficult and that buyers were running for cover.
Even though traders are voicing less optimism on exports, a sentiment encouraged by the EU's lackluster tender award, the big shipments are still going ahead, they said.
Some 50,000 tonnes was loaded in Tilbury this week for Sri Lanka, they said. And a further 25,000 tonnes, at least, is likely to load for Tunisia soon, one said.
But smaller shipments have slowed. "It's the smaller shipments to places like Portugal that seem to have stopped," one said.
Spanish dealers said farmers were increasingly worried by the lack of rain, reflected in higher ex-farm prices in the week to April 4.
Wheat suffered the most, and dealers said the crop in the south may have been damaged now. In other areas, farmers have been holding back supplies for fear of a lower harvest.
While feed wheat prices bounced 1,000 pesetas per tonne to an average of 25,500, milling wheat ex-farm prices were in the 26,500 to 27,000 region, dealers said.
Traders said although there had been some demand for durum wheat, there had been no supply and therefore no prices were available.
Barley also climbed higher to 21,800 peseta per tonne.
Maize was less affected by the lack of rain as it is only just being sown and is grown in irrigated land, dealers said.
Italian durum and soft wheat prices rose over the past week along with foreign wheat prices.

Dealers noted there has been concern over the amount of durum wheat still available on the market. "Only French durum wheat seems available at the moment and this is making Italian durum wheat prices rise," one dealer said.

"In addition to this, pasta exports are also higher causing an increase in demand for durum wheat. The price rise is attributable to a combination of these factors and it seems like this should continue for the next few months," the dealer added.
